intro: Luke Faulkner plays a nocturne whose F♯-major song grows increasingly extravagant, then breaks into a quick, murmuring middle. Even the return has fresh ornaments to spare.

sections.label: A · Song with curling ornaments
sections.mNote: The right hand sings above widely spaced bass and chords

sections.label: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
sections.mNote: Dotted rhythms over quick inner notes and a leaping bass

sections.label: A′ · The ornamented song returns
sections.mNote: The opening melody comes back with new flourishes

cues.title: A small upward turn
cues.text: The melody begins with A♯ nudging up to B, then falls through the notes of a C♯ chord. A deep C♯ in the left hand keeps the phrase waiting; F♯ arrives in the next bar. The little turn already sounds like someone taking breath to sing.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–2: A♯–B upbeat, C♯ bass in bar 1, F♯ bass in bar 2. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: For Ferdinand Hiller
cues.text: Chopin dedicates the three nocturnes of Op. 15, published in 1833–34, to the German pianist Ferdinand Hiller. In a joint letter to Hiller of 20 June 1833 he writes that Liszt is at that moment playing his études, “transporting me outside of my respectable thoughts”.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, Nocturnes, Op. 15: composed 1830–33, first published 1833–34, dedicated to Ferdinand Hiller: https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes,_Op.15_(Chopin,_Frédéric). Chopin, Liszt and Franchomme to Hiller, Paris, 20 June 1833, letter 76 in Chopin’s Letters, coll. Henryk Opienski, trans. E. L. Voynich (New York: Knopf, 1931), pp. 170–71: https://archive.org/details/chopinsletters00chop

cues.title: F♯ turns minor
cues.text: The opening song has a troubled companion in F♯ minor. Its phrases climb high, then spill down in little runs marked dolcissimo, very sweetly. The bass keeps moving beneath those long upper notes.
cues.evidence: Mieczysław Tomaszewski identifies the F♯-minor counter-theme and its rising and falling phrases: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173. Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 17–24: https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twice as fast
cues.text: Doppio movimento: twice the motion, with the piano still speaking sotto voce. A dotted melody rides above quick notes in the same hand while the bass jumps below. The storm starts as a murmur.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32, marked doppio movimento and sotto voce. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A breath before the song
cues.text: The quick figures slow and sink towards the middle of the keyboard. A pause makes room for the opening A♯–B turn. The Larghetto song returns, with new curls of small notes woven into the familiar phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52: molto rallentando, smorzando, a pause, a Tempo and the ornamented reprise. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano and film music
cues.text: Faulkner’s training takes him from piano and composition at Chetham’s to music at Oxford, then screen composition at Edinburgh. He graduates there in 2014, having studied recording and engineering as well as writing music for film.
cues.evidence: Luke Faulkner’s own biography gives his studies at Chetham’s, Oxford and Edinburgh, including the 2014 screen-composition degree: https://www.lukefaulkner.com/about

transitions.title: C♯ beneath the quickened melody
transitions.to: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
transitions.how: Repeated A♯s hold up the end of the slow section. The bass then moves to C♯, with E♯, G♯ and B above it: a dominant seventh. Chopin marks the new passage doppio movimento and sotto voce. The right hand now has a dotted tune and quick notes beneath it; the left hand makes wide jumps.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 24–26. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

transitions.title: A pause, then A♯–B
transitions.from: B · Twice as fast, sotto voce
transitions.how: Over a low C♯, the repeated figures slow and die away: molto rallentando, smorzando. The bass falls silent, and a pause separates the last figure from the opening A♯–B upbeat. Marked a Tempo, the melody returns over C♯ and reaches the F♯ bass in the following bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–50. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
